name: Artemether/lumefantrine
drug_class: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT): artemisinin derivative plus aryl-amino alcohol
route_note: six doses over 3 days, taken with fat-containing food or milk; dispersible tablets for children
targets: Haem detoxification in the parasite food vacuole (lumefantrine)
originator: Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing (Zhou Yiqing and colleagues); developed with Novartis
owner: Novartis (Coartem); WHO-prequalified generics from several manufacturers

discovery.by: Zhou Yiqing and colleagues, Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing
discovery.note: Lumefantrine (benflumetol) was synthesised in China in the 1970s and combined with artemether into a fixed-dose tablet in the 1990s.

tagline: World's most used malaria treatment: a fast artemisinin with a long-acting partner
summary: Artemether/lumefantrine is a fixed-dose artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for uncomplicated malaria. Artemether kills parasites very quickly, while the longer-lived lumefantrine eliminates those that remain. It is the most widely used malaria treatment in Africa, and Novartis supplies it at cost in malaria-endemic countries.
mechanism: Artemisinins contain an endoperoxide bridge that is activated by ferrous iron and haem released when the parasite digests haemoglobin. Activation generates carbon-centred free radicals that alkylate haem and many parasite proteins, causing widespread damage and very rapid killing of blood-stage parasites, including young ring stages. Artemether is converted to dihydroartemisinin, which has a half-life of only an hour or two.

Lumefantrine, a lipophilic aryl-amino alcohol related to mefloquine and halofantrine, is thought to bind haem and block haemozoin formation. Its long half-life clears residual parasites and protects artemether from resistance. Partial artemisinin resistance linked to PfKelch13 mutations, first seen in Southeast Asia, has emerged in East Africa.
uses: Treatment of acute uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in adults and children weighing at least 5 kg (with newer formulations for smaller infants)
Uncomplicated mixed infections including P. falciparum
Completion of treatment after parenteral therapy for severe malaria

history.title: Artemisinin isolated
history.detail: Tu Youyou's team in Project 523 isolates artemisinin from sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua).

history.title: First registration
history.detail: Novartis registers the fixed-dose combination as Coartem/Riamet.

history.title: WHO agreement
history.detail: Novartis agrees to supply Coartem at cost to the public sector in endemic countries; it is added to the WHO Model List in 2002.

history.title: Dispersible form and US approval
history.detail: Coartem Dispersible for children is approved by Swissmedic, and the FDA approves Coartem as the first artemisinin-based drug in the US.

history.title: Nobel Prize
history.detail: Tu Youyou receives the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of artemisinin.

history.title: African resistance
history.detail: Studies confirm PfKelch13 mutations associated with partial artemisinin resistance in Rwanda and Uganda.

history.title: Neonatal formulation
history.detail: Swissmedic approves Coartem Baby, the first malaria treatment for newborns and young infants under 5 kg.

pk.half_life: artemether and dihydroartemisinin about 1–2 h; lumefantrine about 3–6 days
pk.bioavailability: variable; lumefantrine absorption greatly increased by dietary fat
pk.metabolism: artemether CYP3A4 to dihydroartemisinin; lumefantrine CYP3A4

serious: reduced efficacy if not taken with food

facts: Coartem was the first fixed-dose ACT to be prequalified by WHO.
Hundreds of millions of treatment courses have been delivered to endemic countries without profit since 2001.
